  - So it writes zeros from `mFields.m8[11]` down to `mFields.m8[0]` (12 bytes)

When `ch == ':'` and `count == 0`, we set `colonp = dst`. But `dst` is currently pointing to where the NEXT write would go (it was already incremented past the last written bytes). So `colonp` points to the position AFTER the last written byte.

Then in the `::` expansion:
```cpp
while (colonp && dst > colonp)
{
    *endp-- = *dst--;
}
```

This copies bytes from `dst` down to `colonp + 1` to the end of the buffer. But `dst` is the current write position, and `colonp` is where the `::` was seen. So it copies the bytes AFTER the `::` to the end of the buffer.

But what if `colonp` is at `mFields.m8 - 1` (from `::` at the very beginning)? Then `dst` could be at `mFields.m8 + 13` (after writing 7 groups). The loop copies from `dst` down to `colonp + 1 = mFields.m8` to `endp` down. So it copies 14 bytes from `mFields.m8[0..13]` to `mFields.m8[2..15]` (since `endp` starts at `mFields.m8 + 15`). ```cpp

This copies `*dst` to `*endp`, then decrements both. So it copies bytes from the end of the written region to the end of the buffer, working backwards. This is correct for expanding `::`.

But what if `endp` was already decremented by the IPv4 handling? If `hasIp4` is true, `endp -= 4` → `endp = mFields.m8 + 11`. Then the `::` expansion would write to `mFields.m8[11]` down to... but `dst` might be at `mFields.m8 + 13`, and `colonp` at `mFields.m8 - 1`. So the loop would copy from `mFields.m8[13]` down to `mFields.m8[0]` to `mFields.m8[11]` down to... `mFields.m8[-2]`? That would be a buffer underflow on the source side, not a stack overflow.

So it copies from `mFields.m8[13]` down to `mFields.m8[0]` to `mFields.m8[11]` down to `mFields.m8[-2]`. Writing to `mFields.m8[-2]` is a buffer UNDERFLOW (writing before the buffer), not overflow.
